opportunities.title: Invoice Autopilot: a multi-rail 'pay this invoice' router with AP policy and receipts
opportunities.why_it_could_win: Paying invoices is a daily, high-value B2B need, and it fits 'checkout, invoicing, and payment flows' directly. It turns PayBox's passkey approvals into AP controls. It spans multiple rails and complements the curated x402 services instead of cloning one. It also composes core tools (list_requests, get_portfolio, get_buy_link) in an obvious way.
opportunities.feasibility_notes: Request Network calls need x-client-id and an Origin header (owner brokered header), which works because the payer only needs the token. ERC-20 approvals are separate proposals, so up to 2 approvals per invoice. Chains are limited to PayBox's set (Base, Arbitrum, Polygon, Ethereum; Solana); Optimism, BSC and Tron Request Network invoices cannot be paid. Merchant co-signed Solana Pay transaction requests are incompatible: PayBox requires a single signer and no pre-signing. The plugin keeps no state, so duplicate detection must come from inputs or on-chain reads. Hosts: api.hel.io, api.request.network and an RPC host for checks; well under 16.

opportunities.title: Commission Studio: budgeted, verified creative commissions paid over x402
opportunities.description:
Quote, pay, collect, keep.
- quote_commission(brief, medium, budget, deadline): sends unpaid POSTs to StableStudio's 402 challenges to get exact prices and ETAs per model. The response's checkout_session metadata helps here. Returns ranked options within budget.
- commission(option): returns an x402 proposal (POST JSON body, maxAmount = quoted price, Base or Solana).
- collect(jobId, siwx): polls GET /api/jobs/{id} with a SIGN-IN-WITH-X header. The header is built from a CAIP-122 message that the agent signs through core request_wallet_sign (EIP-191).
- keep(url): buys a 6-month StableUpload slot ($0.02 per 10MB) via x402, then copies the image before the roughly 20-minute URL expiry.
- Optional publish: Zora createCoinCall as one Base EVM proposal, with the user as platformReferrer.
Add a delivery verifier (content-type, dimensions, duration) and a brand-kit or style memory passed in as input.
opportunities.why_it_could_win: It matches the Creative track wording almost word for word ('commission and pay for directly'). It shows the full PayBox surface: x402 proposal, core signing for SIWX, EVM proposal, approvals. The demo leaves a tangible asset and a permanent link. Budget routing and delivery verification address a documented x402 problem (sellers taking payment without delivering) instead of just wrapping a single model.
opportunities.feasibility_notes: Hosts: stablestudio.dev, stableupload.dev, the Vercel Blob/S3 upload host, plus Zora's API if used. The 10s limit is fine for probes, polls and image copies. Video re-hosting may exceed 10s, so link out or use short tiers. Generation is asynchronous: images take about 3-10s, video 30s to 5 min. The SIWX polling signature adds one more agent-run step, which is a passkey prompt under always_approve. Dependence on Merit's service is a single-vendor risk; consider a second backend (the builder's own fal/Runway x402 wrapper) to make it 'your product'.

opportunities.title: Brief-to-Merch: the agent designs, pays for and ships physical merch (builder-owned x402 store)
opportunities.description:
Turn a creative brief into a real product.
1. Generate the design (Commission Studio or your own wrapper).
2. Create a Printful mockup.
3. quote_merch(design_url, sku, size, ship_to) returns an exact total: the Printful estimate plus shipping plus margin.
4. Pay with an x402 proposal to the builder's own endpoint, which settles via the Coinbase facilitator or Stripe x402. Alternatively, use a MoonPay Commerce dynamic paylink.
5. On settlement, the builder's backend confirms the Printful order.
6. track_order returns status and tracking.
Metadata can be left optional, but the order is real.
opportunities.why_it_could_win: Real-world fulfillment is what agents actually pay for: gift cards and prepaid cards dominate x402 revenue, while data resale does not. A physical object designed by an agent makes a memorable X demo. It is clearly 'your product' and covers the Creative and Merchant tracks at once, on MoonPay-aligned rails.
opportunities.feasibility_notes: Needs a small backend: an x402 server plus the Printful API key. Printful charges the builder's billing method only when an order is confirmed, so the builder is merchant of record and owns taxes and returns. Shipping addresses pass through tool input as PII: minimize them and never log them. Delivery takes longer than the hackathon, so show the confirmed order and tracking. Limit scope to 1-2 SKUs. The plugin only proposes payment, and fulfillment happens server-side after settlement, so no plugin state is needed.

opportunities.title: Escrowed Commissions: agents hire human creators with on-chain buyer protection
opportunities.why_it_could_win: This would be the first non-custodial 'agent pays a human' flow with refunds in the PayBox marketplace. It fills the 'stablecoins have no chargebacks' gap that matters for merchant tools, and it is the 'paying humans' angle for Creative. It differs from RentAHuman (custodial wallet, 18% fee). It uses audited Coinbase/Base contracts instead of a hackathon escrow contract, which helps on compliance and technical-execution judging.
opportunities.feasibility_notes: Contracts are already deployed: AuthCaptureEscrow v1.1.0 on Base. The builder needs an operator relayer key plus gas, and a creator-facing page. EIP-712 signing has to be done by the agent through the core tool, because a plugin cannot request signatures. The transaction window will not decode escrow semantics, so the plugin must return precise summaries. This is the highest build complexity of the list: tight for one person in 36h, and the demo needs a real creator (the builder or a friend).

opportunities.title: Exact-total universal checkout on crypto rails (Rye x402), with a card 'quote-and-bind' fallback
opportunities.description: search: Shopify Global Catalog MCP (seller domain, variants), or the product URL directly. create_intent: x402 proposal (Rye, $0.02) carrying product URL, quantity and buyer/shipping info. get_offer: free polling returns the exact total, including tax and shipping. confirm: x402 proposal with maxAmount = offer total + $0.03. order_status and shipments: free reads. Card fallback when crypto is not possible: return the canonical merchant_url origin (seller domain) and exact amount_cents, ready for core request_payment.
opportunities.why_it_could_win: It is a 'buy almost anything' demo where the user sees the exact landed cost before a single approval, across 15,000+ merchants, on Base or Solana. It treats PayBox's approval window as the spending cap.
opportunities.feasibility_notes: Verify that x402.rye.com is live and that its request schema fits PayBox's no-custom-header POST: the hostname did not resolve from this research sandbox, possibly due to local DNS limits. Shipping is US-centric. It overlaps PayBox launch partner Purch.xyz (Amazon over Solana x402), so it needs clear differentiation: catalog breadth, landed-cost transparency, tracking. Shopify Catalog requires a hosted UCP agent profile URL. Physical delivery takes longer than the hackathon.

opportunities.title: Card Checkout Copilot: quote-and-bind for PayBox's merchant-bound one-time cards
opportunities.why_it_could_win: It is uniquely PayBox. One-time cards bound to merchant and amount only work if the binding origin and the amount are right, which are exactly the steps agents get wrong. It extends PayBox to any card-accepting merchant without the plugin touching credentials.
opportunities.feasibility_notes:
High demo risk:
- Claude.ai and ChatGPT web connectors cannot reliably drive web checkouts.
- 3DS, CAPTCHAs and bot detection apply.
- Shopify Checkout MCP needs a Dev Dashboard bearer token and a Shopify-Buyer-IP header, which the plugin sandbox cannot legitimately supply, and general access ends at continue_url anyway.
- request_payment is USD only.
Best used as a secondary path inside another plugin, not as the headline.

opportunities.title: Agent-ready creator storefront: sell licensed digital goods to agents
opportunities.description: The builder hosts x402 endpoints selling licensed digital goods: their own or CC0 stock photos, sample packs, style or prompt packs, with license terms in a machine-readable receipt. Settlement goes through Stripe machine payments (x402 on Base, paid out in fiat to the Stripe balance) or MoonPay Commerce paylinks. Plugin tools: search_catalog, get_license_terms, buy_license (x402 proposal). The paid response returns a signed license receipt and a StableUpload download URL.
opportunities.why_it_could_win: It covers the merchant side ('let a business accept agent payments') together with creative licensing, a genuinely missing supply category. Fiat settlement through Stripe makes it credible for real businesses.
opportunities.feasibility_notes: Needs an x402 server (Coinbase facilitator or Stripe). Stripe stablecoin acceptance requires review, and covers US businesses except New York. Content rights are mandatory under the hackathon terms. Evidence of demand for paid creative goods is thin, so frame it around a concrete buyer workflow (an agent assembling a deck or video and licensing assets inline).

avoid: A single-model 'AI image/video generator' x402 wrapper: crowded (StableStudio, AgentUtility, x402.press, Gondola). PayBox core use_service can already pay these, and agents are instructed to offer both catalogs, so a thin plugin adds nothing.
Another gift-card or prepaid-card plugin: Bitrefill and Laso already dominate x402 revenue with mature price-locked invoices, and Bitrefill is reachable via discover_services.
An undifferentiated Amazon/Shopify 'buy anything' plugin: Purch.xyz is a PayBox launch integration and Rye already sells checkout over x402.
Restaurant reservations or flights: AgentRes.dev and BRIJ.fi are PayBox launch integrations, and Resy-based booking carries account-ban risk.

Any plugin that receives raw card numbers or CVC as tool input, or drives browser checkout with them: risks disqualification for credential misuse, pulls the plugin into PCI scope, cannot fit the 10s budget, and runs into bot detection and 3DS.
Building on Shopify Checkout MCP complete_checkout: limited to trusted tiers, needs a Shopify-Buyer-IP the sandbox cannot legitimately supply, and general access ends at continue_url.
Story Protocol licensing: Story's L1 is not a PayBox chain, so there is no single-proposal path, and its docs served an expired TLS certificate at fetch time.
Unofficial Suno or Udio wrappers: no official API, plus IP and ToS risk that conflicts with the third-party-rights clause in the hackathon terms.
Sub-cent micropayment products: a flat facilitation fee of about $0.003 exceeds the price of the goods.
Reselling free data (weather, prices, balances): independent testing found it adds fragility, not value.
Cloudflare AI Gateway x402 as a backend: needs a Cloudflare API token header, US residency and a card on file, and PayBox x402 proposals forbid custom headers.
Merchant tools that need each user's own API keys (MoonPay Commerce, Request Network, Printful, RentAHuman): plugin secrets belong to the owner, and plugins cannot read users' PayBox secrets.
Making creator-coin or memecoin launches the core feature: compliance and 'speculation' optics. Keep Zora as an optional publish step.
Multi-payee splits that rely on batching: PayBox allows one call per proposal, so N payees means N approvals unless you call a pre-existing splitter contract.
constraints_risks: Each call gets 10 seconds in a fresh sandbox, so all generation and checkout must be asynchronous. Carry state as IDs passed back by the agent, on-chain records, or provider-side jobs.
x402 payments complete after the sandbox exits and the plugin is never resumed. Design two-step tools (pay, then collect), with the agent passing the paid response or job ID into the next call.

SIWX-gated retrieval (StableStudio jobs, Bitrefill redemption codes, StableUpload owner actions) needs signatures that only the agent can obtain via request_wallet_sign. That is an extra step and possibly another passkey prompt.
Plugin money tools always require user approval, even under autonomous grants. Design for one approval per real spend, and avoid flows that need several approve-then-pay pairs.
The EVM transaction window shows only raw calldata. Users rely on the plugin's summary, which PayBox treats as untrusted, so summaries must be exact and checkable.
The plugin cannot choose the wallet. The agent must pass the payer or sender address: MoonPay Commerce needs it as payerAddress, and Solana proposals need it as sender.
Brokered API credentials belong to the plugin owner, so every third-party call is billed to and authenticated as the builder. That rules out multi-tenant merchant tools that use each user's own keys.
Delivery risk: about 11% of judgeable paid x402 endpoints did not return the fields they promised. Verify deliverables before declaring success, and avoid relying on a single provider.
Generated asset URLs expire (about 20 minutes for StableStudio). Persist them immediately; large videos may not fit the 10s re-host window.
Physical goods take longer to arrive than the hackathon lasts. Shipping addresses are personal data passing through tool inputs, so minimize and never log them.

Market evidence: x402 settlement is volatile (reported down 93% year to date on Base-scope data), creative x402 revenue is tiny, and 92% of buyers stick to one seller. Distribution through the PayBox marketplace, rather than raw x402 listings, is the realistic channel.

Execution limits: plugin calls are capped at 1 start per second and 1,000 per rolling 24h; transaction validation allows 1 active and 30 per hour; the bundle must be at most 10 MiB; one project per participant; MoonPay KYC may gate eligibility; a live end-to-end demo must be posted on X.
Compliance: you must hold rights to third-party APIs and content, follow provider ToS (scraping and automated booking are risky), and show meaningful human contribution, or risk disqualification.
open_questions: Does PayBox's x402 handling (plugin proposals and use_service) support x402 v2 extensions such as sign-in-with-x, the 'upto' scheme, or MPP challenges? Or must the agent always sign SIWX manually?
The plugin guide mentions a 'proposal amount limit'. What is the maximum USDC amount per plugin money proposal, and per grant?

Can plugin tool results include MCP image content or resource links that Claude, ChatGPT or Grok render inline? This matters for creative previews, and the docs only mention text plus structured data.
Is there a timeout on PayBox's paid re-fetch for x402 proposals? It decides whether synchronous slow-generation endpoints are viable.
Will judges count a plugin that orchestrates third-party x402 services (StableStudio, Rye, Bitrefill) as 'your product', or do they expect a builder-owned service behind it?
Are StableStudio, Rye, Bitrefill or MoonPay Commerce already in PayBox's curated discover_services set? Overlap changes how much a plugin adds.
Does PayBox's plugin and gateway egress share IP addresses across users? MoonPay Commerce rate-limits per IP at 10 requests per 60s.
Is x402.rye.com live and reachable with a body-only POST and no API key? DNS did not resolve from this research sandbox.
Can a hackathon participant create MoonPay Commerce paylinks without KYB (dashboard only)? Is the partner x-merchant-id mode available for multi-merchant tools?

How does PayBox's one-time card behave when the final merchant charge differs from amount_cents (tax, shipping, tips, currency)? Can it be used for API credit top-ups at merchants like ElevenLabs or fal?
Is there any x402 or agent-API ticketing rail for the 'concert tickets' job the PayBox manual mentions? None was verified, because the WebSearch quota ran out during this research.
Not verified for the same quota reason: Coinbase Business or Sphere invoicing APIs, x402 stock-media or music-licensing sellers, and Duffel payment flows for agents.

summary:
Verdict: a hosted plugin is a stateless stdio MCP server. It speaks protocol 2026-07-28 and runs in a fresh sandbox for every operation, with a hard 10 s budget that includes startup. A winning design keeps the plugin thin: validate input, make one or two bounded fetches (4 s or less), then return either text plus structured data or one proposal. State and slow work go to a companion API on a configured host, authenticated with a brokered header.

Chains:
- Solana proposals work on mainnet only.
- x402 works only with USDC on Base mainnet or Solana mainnet.
- EVM proposals accept any eip155 ID by syntax, but the network must be 'available in PayBox'. The app's PORTFOLIO_CHAINS list has Ethereum, Base, BNB, Polygon, Optimism, Arbitrum, Avalanche, Robinhood Chain (4663), Arc (5042), Hyperliquid (999) and Solana.
- Base is the safest target: it has the documented examples, the x402 rail and the default buy-link. No testnets are exposed, so build and demo with small mainnet amounts.

What matters most in MCP 2026-07-28 is what PayBox does not negotiate. Conformance sends clientCapabilities {} and requires resultType 'complete'. So MRTR (multi-round-trip requests, the new elicitation path), the tasks extension, sampling, x-mcp-header and custom UI are all unavailable. Use explicit handles (the spec's 'Stateful Tools' guidance) and submit-then-poll tools. outputSchema and structuredContent are first-class, and a proposal must be declared inline under io.paybox/transactionProposal.

Identity: the plugin never sees who the user is or which wallet_id they chose, so any address argument is unauthenticated. Options:
1. Address-keyed data for public reads only.
2. High-entropy bearer handles minted by your backend, for example returned inside the paid x402 response.
3. A SIWE-style handshake: core request_wallet_sign, then the backend verifies and issues a short-lived token.
4. On-chain state where the contract enforces msg.sender.

Upstash REST and Alchemy accept Bearer headers, so they work as brokered hosts.

EIP-712 composition (the plugin returns typed data, the agent signs it with core typedData, a second plugin tool relays it) works mechanically. It mirrors the documented step where the agent passes a paid response into the next plugin call. But PayBox doesn't document it, it takes several steps, and reviewers may see it as getting around the rule that plugin money tools always need approval. Prefer flows with no off-chain signature: CoW Protocol PreSign turns an intent order into one setPreSignature call. A Polymarket relay is a trap: ClobAuth plus per-user HMAC secrets, and an IP geoblock that would apply to PayBox's own egress.

Stack:
- Hono on Cloudflare Workers or Vercel, with @x402/* 2.28 (v2 headers) and the PayAI facilitator (no key) or CDP's.
- Never the x402.org facilitator; it is testnet-only.
- Foundry to Base for small contracts.
- Avoid custom Solana programs: rent is about 6.96 SOL per MB.

Demo host: use the Claude.ai connector. The signing window renders at once and use_plugin accepts wallet_id. Avoid:
- Grok: it draws the window only after the reply finishes.
- Claude Code: it can refuse before the tool call.
- CLI hosts: the SDK and CLI can't pass wallet_id, and the SDK driver can't complete x402 or gasless plugin plans.

Submit early. End-to-end agent testing only works after Submit Project puts the plugin under Unofficial plugins. Code freezes at the deadline; hosts, variables and secrets stay editable.

(Process note: two SDK bundle copies were saved to the session scratchpad, /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-oluwademilade-Desktop-paybox/025994f1-f93a-49c4-857a-bb9ba7e918e6/scratchpad/sdk/, so they could be read.)

key_facts.fact: Starter 1.0.2 pins protocolVersion 2026-07-28, Node 24.21.0, pnpm 11.11.0, @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.0.0, zod 4.4.3, esbuild 0.28.2. The plugin serves over stdio via serveStdio(createServer, { legacy: 'reject' }), which rejects 2025-era initialize openings, and the build is a single esbuild ESM bundle (target node24).

Local conformance sends each tools/list or tools/call with _meta io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion, clientInfo and clientCapabilities {} (no initialize handshake). It fails unless result.resultType === 'complete', and it rejects any inputSchema containing x-mcp-header.

Hosted limits: bundle up to 10 MiB UTF-8; stdout 256 KiB and stderr 16 KiB per operation; 10 s per operation; 16 tool-list pages and 256 tools; 64 KiB combined input+output schema per tool; 128-byte tool names; 1 KiB cursors; 64 KiB sample arguments; 128 result content blocks.

Each discovery page and call may run in a fresh process. Keep network calls out of module startup and discovery, use bounded requests (the guide suggests a 4 s fetch timeout; examples use AbortSignal.timeout(4000) and redirect:'error'). Platform failures during discovery may be retried up to 3 times.

Network access is limited to exact configured hostnames: up to 16, with no wildcards or redirect chains. API keys are host-scoped brokered headers (up to 16) that PayBox injects; the plugin never reads them. Env vars are for non-sensitive config only. Output containing the literal value of a brokered credential is withheld.

Plugin calls, hosted tests and checks share a per-user allowance of 1 start per second and 1,000 per rolling 24 h. Transaction validation is separately limited to 1 active and 30 per hour, and each result can be validated once within 5 minutes.

End-to-end agent testing requires Submit Project: the plugin then appears under 'Unofficial plugins' and can be enabled privately. The portal's Validate transaction only simulates and never signs or broadcasts. After the deadline you cannot upload, submit or withdraw, but you can still edit network hosts, variables and secrets, and installed plugins use the owner's latest config on new calls.

EVM proposal shape: kind 'evm', canonical chain 'eip155:<id>', transaction {to,value,data}. It is one call only, on a network 'available in PayBox'. There are no token/transfer/swap fields and unknown fields are rejected. PayBox does not add approvals, fetch quotes or choose slippage. The helper also enforces calldata of 120 KiB or less, value under 2^256 and chain ID under 2^64.

Solana proposal rules: chain 'solana:mainnet' only; canonical padded Base64 of at most 1,232 decoded bytes; exactly one required signer, who is also the fee payer, with an empty signature slot; legacy or v0 only. No durable nonce, pre-signing, extra signers or sponsor. PayBox replaces the blockhash (a zero placeholder is fine) and re-simulates immediately before signing. The sender public address comes in as a tool argument and is checked against the chosen wallet.

x402 proposal rules: chain eip155:8453 or solana:mainnet; exact USDC assets only (Base 0x8335...2913, Solana EPjF...Dt1v); maxAmount is a positive atomic integer; expiry within 5 min. The request must be HTTPS on port 443, either GET with no body or POST with up to 64 KiB of JSON, with no custom headers or credential injection. The endpoint host must be a configured network host.

x402 lifecycle: PayBox fetches the live 402 and checks asset and amount against the proposal. The sandbox ends before approval, so the agent polls the request ID instead of re-running the tool. The terminal response contains the payment status and the service response; an agent may pass that paid response into a later plugin call. Developer validation sends the unpaid request, which can have provider-side effects.

Proposal envelope: version '1', with expiresAt as a whole-second UTC timestamp within 5 minutes (helpers default to 4). It must not contain wallet IDs, signing keys, approval modes, signatures, RPC URLs or broadcast instructions. Tool text is treated as untrusted. The transaction window shows network, sender and raw details (for EVM, also destination and value in wei) with no decoded ERC-20, allowance or swap summary.

Before signing an EVM proposal, PayBox refreshes the nonce and rechecks execution without raising the approved fee limits. Once signing starts the prepared transaction is frozen. Success means the transaction is confirmed on-chain, not just broadcast; pending_confirmation means the outcome is still being reconciled.

The starter's evmOutputSchema, solanaOutputSchema and x402OutputSchema are strict zod objects containing only the 'io.paybox/transactionProposal' key. Returning extra structured fields next to a proposal therefore needs a custom inline schema.

Wallet choice: for installed Open Plugins the agent sets use_plugin.wallet_id next to plugin_id, tool_id and input. PayBox never sends that ID to plugin code. It can be omitted when the user has one compatible wallet and is required with several; the plugin cannot choose.

In @paybox-sh/sdk 2.2.0 (published 2026-10-14), UsePluginArgs is { pluginId, toolId, input, invocationId } with no walletId, and the CLI 'paybox plugins use <plugin-id> <tool-id>' only offers --input and --invocation-id. CLI and SDK hosts therefore cannot pass wallet_id.

The SDK runPlugin/resumeRequest driver signs only validated EVM or Solana transaction plans. Unknown formats, versioned plans and gasless prepared plans return outcome 'unsupported'. Funding needs return pending_funding with reason 'funding_required'. 'terminal' is reported only when the success output carries a tx_hash or signature.

use_plugin results carry _meta 'com.moonpay.paybox/invocationId' and 'com.moonpay.paybox/requestId'. Passing invocation_id again retrieves the same ambiguous unofficial-plugin call. A core 'reopen_signing_window' tool exists, and request statuses include 'pending_funding'.

discover_plugins takes query, source (all|official|user), status (all|enabled|disabled), limit (default 10, max 25) and cursor. Results carry id, type (official|unofficial), enabled, contract_uri and protocol_version; unofficial results include tool schemas directly. Official plugins are read via get_contract(contract_uri). Disabled plugins expose an enable_url.

Naming is inconsistent: the developer guide tells agents to use discover_plugins and get_plugin for installed plugins, while the docs and SDK expose get_contract. The guide also says 'remote plugins use their connected origin' for x402, which implies a remote-plugin model it doesn't document.
Plugin money tools always pause for the user's approval, even under an autonomous grant. Approvals are bound to the exact operation and expire after about 10 minutes.

The PayBox web app bundle defines PORTFOLIO_CHAINS as Ethereum 1, Base 8453, BNB 56, Polygon 137, Optimism 10, Arbitrum 42161, Avalanche 43114, Robinhood Chain 4663, Arc 5042, Hyperliquid 999 and Solana (network ID 1399811149). A second name map also includes Monad 143 and Celo 42220. These are display maps, used here as a proxy for 'available in PayBox'.
At launch (2026-07-29) MoonPay listed Solana plus Ethereum, Hyperliquid, Tempo, Base, Robinhood Chain, Arbitrum and Polygon, 'with more coming'.
SDK buy-link destinations are typed as eip155:8453 | eip155:1 | eip155:4663 | solana:mainnet. Chain 4663 is Robinhood Chain and 5042 is Arc, whose native gas token is USDC.
The docs give Hyperliquid as eip155:999 ('hyperevm' alias) and name Robinhood, Arc and Hyperliquid as featured networks. An EVM MPC wallet uses one address across every eip155 chain.
The host-facing PayBox MCP endpoint is streamable HTTP on protocol 2025-06-18, and the SDK's MCP client sends PROTOCOL_VERSION 2025-06-18. Plugins are a separate surface on 2026-07-28.
x402 requires a plain EOA payer. If the wallet is EIP-7702 delegated, PayBox either returns an error or, where auto-undelegate is enabled for that chain, runs a composite flow that undelegates first.

Core request_wallet_sign ops and their outputs: message (EIP-191); typedData (EIP-712, returns {signature}); transaction (EIP-1559, returns a serializedTransaction that is not broadcast); authorization (EIP-7702); solanaMessage; solanaTransaction (returns signedTransactionBase64); raw digest. The SDK's signing core has no typedData allow-list.

The curated discover_services list only shows x402 services with at least 10 unique payers in the last 30 days on a supported rail; raw:true returns the uncurated catalog. Core use_service supports custom headers and a probe mode (MCP-only), unlike plugin x402 proposals.

Host routing: Claude.ai, ChatGPT web and grok.com use the MCP connector; Muse, Grok Bot and Grok Computer must use the CLI. Grok draws the signing window only after the agent's reply finishes. Claude Code can refuse financial operations before any tool call; the docs recommend Claude chat as the workaround.

The SKILL.md host table gives Muse link_surface=phone_browser, no buttons and no kept process. Grok Bot gets link_surface=app, renders buttons and keeps the process, but login is not allowed from group chats.

Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, announced 2026-09-08. It runs in a dedicated 'Muse Secure VM' with its own browser, gated by a separate Sentinel agent, and is rolling out in the US on iOS, Android and muse.ai.

Grok Bot is xAI's product for durable named Bots, with memory, a shared computer, skills, routines, group chats and a marketplace. MoonPay's public paybox-plugin repo is currently packaged as a Grok plugin.
Grok Computer is xAI's PC-control agent. An enable_grok_computer flag was found in March 2026 and Musk said 'coming out soon'. PayBox docs now list it as a CLI host, but no launch was confirmed.

MCP 2026-07-28 changes:
- The core is stateless: no initialize, and every request carries _meta protocolVersion and clientCapabilities.
- Servers must implement server/discover.
- Results carry resultType 'complete' or 'input_required'; MRTR replaces server-initiated elicitation, sampling and roots.
- Tasks moved to the io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension (polled with tasks/get).
- Roots, Sampling and Logging are deprecated.
- List results carry ttlMs and cacheScope.
- x-mcp-header was added.
- inputSchema and outputSchema may use any JSON Schema 2020-12, and structuredContent may be any JSON value.

The spec's 'Stateful Tools' guidance says to return an explicit handle from a creation tool and accept it on later calls. For unauthenticated servers the handle is a bearer token: give it high entropy (for example UUIDv4) and a bounded lifetime, and return a tool error on expired handles.

@modelcontextprotocol/server 2.0.0 was published 2026-07-27; the latest is 2.3.1 (2026-10-05). v2 is the stable line implementing 2026-07-28, replaces the monolithic @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, and ships ajv and cf-worker validators plus stdio entry points.

x402 v2 packages: @x402/core, evm, svm, hono, express, next and fetch are at 2.28.0 (2026-09-29), and the repo moved to x402-foundation. The flow uses PAYMENT-REQUIRED and PAYMENT-SIGNATURE headers. Schemes are exact, upto and batch-settlement. Self-facilitation inside the resource server is supported.

The x402.org facilitator is testnet-only and must not be used for mainnet routes. Mainnet examples are https://api.cdp.coinbase.com/platform/v2/x402 and https://facilitator.payai.network. Solana mainnet's CAIP-2 ID is solana:5eykt4UsFv8P8NJdTREpY1vzqKqZKvdp, and routes can register eip155:* and solana:* wildcards.
The PayAI facilitator needs no API key for ordinary exact payments, and its free tier gives 1,000 credits per receiving wallet. It also exposes a Bazaar discovery endpoint.
The CDP facilitator requires CDP API keys, runs KYT/OFAC checks, and is reported as fee-free on Base and Solana mainnet. The CDP docs could not be fetched directly.
Cloudflare Workers Free allows 10 ms CPU per request, 50 subrequests and 100k requests per day; Paid allows 30 s CPU by default. Time spent waiting on the network doesn't count toward CPU.
Vercel Functions on Fluid compute: Hobby allows 300 s duration (default and maximum), request and response bodies are capped at 4.5 MB, and functions run in a single region (iad1) by default.
The Upstash Redis REST API authenticates with 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' and supports /pipeline and /multi-exec, so a plugin can reach it directly through a brokered header.
Alchemy JSON-RPC accepts the API key as an Authorization: Bearer header instead of in the URL path, which makes it brokerable.

CoW Protocol PreSign works for EOAs: POST the order with signingScheme presign, signature 0x and from=owner, then call setPreSignature(orderUid,true) on GPv2Settlement 0x9008D19f58AAbD9eD0D60971565AA8510560ab41. Passing false cancels the order.

CoW's GPv2Settlement and GPv2VaultRelayer (0xC92E8bdf79f0507f65a392b0ab4667716BFE0110) are deployed on Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Polygon, BNB, Avalanche, Optimism, Gnosis, Linea, Ink and Plasma. The orderbook API answered unauthenticated requests on base, polygon and arbitrum_one.

The Polymarket CLOB needs an L1 EIP-712 ClobAuth signature (chain 137) to create or derive API credentials (apiKey, secret, passphrase), then L2 HMAC headers on every private request. Orders also need a wallet signature.

Polymarket's geoblock is based on the requesting IP. The US, UK, France, Germany, Canada (some provinces) and others are close-only on both frontend and API, so orders from blocked regions are rejected.

Jupiter Trigger API v2 order creation needs a depositSignedTx (a signed deposit transaction passed to Jupiter's API), JWT auth and an x-api-key header, with a 10 USD minimum. That is incompatible with PayBox proposals, where PayBox signs and broadcasts.

Solana rent-exempt minimum = (size + 128) × 3,480 lamports per byte-year × 2 years, which is about 6.96 SOL per MB of account data. That makes custom program deployment costly; the cost figure is computed from the formula.
MoonPay's onboarding post says a Claude or ChatGPT account is enough and gives a pre-filled Claude connector link, with Customize → Connectors as the fallback.

opportunities.title: x402 commission-and-poll pipeline (thin plugin, paid backend)
opportunities.description:
Tools:
- quote_job (data tool): validates the request and returns price and ETA from your backend.
- order_job: returns ONE x402 proposal (POST of 64 KiB JSON or less to your own HTTPS endpoint) on Base USDC or Solana USDC.

After payment, your backend (Hono with @x402/hono, @x402/evm and @x402/svm, using the PayAI or CDP facilitator) enqueues the work and returns {job_id, access_token, eta}. That response reaches the agent through the PayBox request. A get_job(job_id, access_token) data tool then polls the backend and returns hosted result URLs, never inline base64.
opportunities.why_it_could_win: It shows the hackathon's own headline ('already wrapped an API in x402? you're halfway there'). It works end to end on both rails, survives the 10 s budget for any slow generative work, and needs no user identity: the payment is the authorization and the handle is a bearer token. The demo is clean: approve the payment, then the result appears.
opportunities.feasibility_notes: Fits every hosted constraint: the payment is a single proposal and the other tools are fast data calls. The 402 must quote at or below maxAmount in exact USDC. The unpaid probe must be side-effect free because portal validation sends it. Keep the paid response small. Poll get_request (core) for payment status and the plugin tool only for job status, to save the 1/s and 1,000/day quota. PayBox's timeout and size cap for the paid re-fetch are unknown, so return quickly. Requires mainnet USDC on a plain-EOA wallet.

opportunities.title: EVM limit / TWAP-style orders via CoW Protocol PreSign
opportunities.description:
Tools:
- create_limit_order: calls CoW /quote, POSTs the order with signingScheme presign, signature 0x and from=user address (passed as an argument), then returns ONE EVM proposal calling GPv2Settlement.setPreSignature(orderUid,true).
- ensure_allowance: returns a separate ERC-20 approve(VaultRelayer) proposal when the allowance is short.
- order_status and cancel_order: setPreSignature(uid,false), or CoW's off-chain cancellation.
opportunities.why_it_could_win: PayBox's integration manual lists 'limit order' jobs as things agents should route to plugins, and core request_swap only does market swaps. CoW gives MEV-protected, solver-filled orders with no EIP-712 composition and no API key. Each step is a legible single call on Base, Arbitrum or Polygon, so it fits Consumer finance.
opportunities.feasibility_notes: Two fast HTTP calls (quote and order) fit within 10 s. orderUid must belong to the msg.sender wallet; a mismatched address argument fails PayBox simulation, which works as a safety net. The approval must confirm before the order can fill. The transaction window shows only raw calldata, so explain the order in tool text. Confirm that eip155:42161 and eip155:137 are accepted in portal validation; Base is the safest.

opportunities.title: x402 merchant invoice / checkout rail
opportunities.description:
Merchant-side tools:
- create_invoice: the backend mints an invoice with a dedicated x402 URL priced in USDC.
- pay_invoice: returns ONE x402 proposal to that URL.
- get_receipt: the backend records the payer address from facilitator settlement and returns a receipt or status.

Refunds can be offered as an EVM USDC transfer proposal from the merchant's own PayBox wallet.
opportunities.why_it_could_win: It hits the Merchant tools track using PayBox's native rail instead of card checkouts, which plugins cannot do. It works for any business with a single HTTPS endpoint, and it needs no per-user secrets.
opportunities.feasibility_notes: Payment rides on PayBox's x402 proposal path: no custom headers, exact USDC, expiry within 5 min. Invoice state lives in the backend (Workers KV, D1, Upstash or Postgres). The payer must be a plain EOA. Use mainnet with small amounts.

opportunities.title: Signature-gated per-user state (SIWE handshake) as a plugin feature
opportunities.description:
Tools:
- auth_challenge(address): the backend returns a SIWE (EIP-4361) message with a nonce.
- The agent signs it with core request_wallet_sign {op:'message'} or solanaMessage.
- auth_verify(address, signature): the backend verifies (viem with ERC-1271/6492 support) and returns a 15–60 minute token.

Later tools (budgets, savings goals, watchlists, rules) take that token. The backend authenticates the plugin itself with a brokered Authorization header.
opportunities.why_it_could_win: It solves the hardest constraint (no state, no identity) safely. It lets a plugin offer persistent, user-specific features that other entries will fake with unauthenticated address keys, and judges score compliance and technical execution.
opportunities.feasibility_notes: The signature costs one signing-window interaction, and the grant may require a passkey. The token sits in model context, so keep it short-lived and narrowly scoped. Make the nonce single-use in the backend. Do not let the token authorize spending; money still goes through PayBox proposals.

opportunities.title: Single-call USDC deposits via EIP-3009 receiveWithAuthorization into your own contract
opportunities.description:
A small Foundry contract on Base (for example a savings jar or escrow) exposes depositWithAuthorization(from, amount, validAfter, validBefore, nonce, v, r, s), which calls USDC.receiveWithAuthorization.
1. The plugin returns typed data for the agent to sign with core typedData.
2. A second tool takes the signature and returns ONE EVM proposal calling depositWithAuthorization.
This removes the separate approve proposal. Withdrawals and settlement are single calls too.
opportunities.why_it_could_win: It turns the 'no batching, approvals must be separate' limit into one clean on-chain action with readable state. It is a strong technical-execution story for Consumer finance or Merchant escrow.
opportunities.feasibility_notes: The composition is mechanically possible but not documented by PayBox. The money still moves through an approved plugin proposal, which keeps it compliant, unlike relaying signatures off-chain. Fall back to approve plus deposit as two proposals if the typedData step proves awkward. Deploying on Base costs cents.

opportunities.title: CREATE2 per-user contracts as durable plugin state
opportunities.description: Deploy a factory once. A plugin tool proposes factory.create(salt=user address, params), a single call. The plugin then computes the user's contract address deterministically from their address and reads its state over a brokered RPC host (for example Alchemy via Bearer header). All later actions are single calls to that contract.
opportunities.why_it_could_win: It gives tamper-proof per-user state and authorization (msg.sender checks) with no backend database or identity layer. It suits vaults, recurring-payment allowances, prediction escrows or subscriptions.
opportunities.feasibility_notes: Proposals require a 'to' address, so direct contract creation is impossible; going through a factory solves that. The 120 KiB calldata cap is ample. Reads must fit within 4 s. Users need gas on the target chain.

avoid: Polymarket CLOB order relay: it needs a ClobAuth EIP-712 signature plus per-user HMAC API secrets the plugin cannot store. The geoblock is IP-based, so orders posted from PayBox's sandbox egress would likely be rejected (US is close-only), which is also a compliance red flag for judges.

Solana limit orders through Jupiter Trigger v2: it requires submitting depositSignedTx and JWT auth to Jupiter, but PayBox signs and broadcasts proposals itself. Only a sign-via-core-then-relay hack would work, and it is undocumented.

Any flow needing several EVM calls to happen atomically (approve+swap, 7702 batches, multicall acting as the user). V1 allows one call per proposal, and a Multicall contract becomes msg.sender instead of the user.

Solana programs or SDKs that need extra signers (fresh keypair accounts, some NFT and position mints), partial pre-signing, durable nonces, fee sponsorship, or transactions over 1,232 bytes. All are rejected; use PDAs or createAccountWithSeed instead.
Doing slow work inside the tool call, such as synchronous AI generation, heavy RPC scans or multiple sequential APIs. The 10 s budget includes sandbox startup; return a handle and poll instead.

Relying on MCP elicitation/MRTR (input_required), the tasks extension, sampling, subscriptions, x-mcp-header, in-memory caches or custom UI. PayBox conformance requires resultType 'complete' and sends empty client capabilities.
APIs that only accept keys in URL query parameters. Brokered secrets are header-only, and env vars are non-sensitive, so these need a proxy on your own host.

Card-checkout plugins. Plugin proposals can only be evm, solana or x402. request_payment is a core agent tool that issues a one-time card and does not complete checkout, and browser checkouts are exposed to merchant bot defenses (an inference).
Testnet-only tooling (x402.org facilitator, Base Sepolia, Solana devnet). PayBox's x402 rails and Solana proposals are mainnet-only.
Swap or bridge wrappers that duplicate core request_swap (MoonX quotes, cross-chain): little novelty, plus allowance and slippage pitfalls.
Returning base64 images or large JSON from tools. Stdout is capped at 256 KiB per operation and results land in model context; return hosted URLs.

Recording the demo on Grok (the signing window appears only after the reply ends), in Claude Code (it may refuse financial operations before any tool call), or on CLI hosts (no wallet_id on use_plugin, and the SDK driver can't complete x402 or gasless plugin plans).
Expecting your new x402 endpoint to appear in curated discover_services. That needs 10 or more unique payers in 30 days; the plugin itself is the discovery path.
constraints_risks: The 10 s per-operation budget includes sandbox startup and module evaluation. Keep the bundle lean, do no network work at import time, and cap each fetch at about 4 s (parallelize with Promise.all).

No persistence and no identity: the plugin sees neither the user's identity nor their wallet_id. Address arguments are unauthenticated, so anything sensitive needs a signature-based handshake or on-chain msg.sender checks.

Builds must be deterministic: pnpm test builds twice and requires identical bytes, so avoid embedded timestamps or random IDs. The bundle must be one UTF-8 dist/plugin.mjs of 10 MiB or less, with all deps bundled.

Network: up to 16 exact hosts and 16 header-only brokered secrets; redirects and wildcards are not supported. The x402 endpoint host must also be configured. Responses that echo a brokered secret are withheld.

Quotas: 1 start per second and 1,000 per 24 h per user, shared by plugin calls, tests and checks. Agents that call tools in parallel, or poll plugin tools in loops, can hit the limit. Validation is capped at 30 per hour.
Expiry: proposals must expire within 5 minutes (helpers use 4), and approvals expire after about 10 minutes. A slow passkey approval can outlive a quote; check the request status before re-proposing.

Simulation must pass with the user's actual wallet: enough gas or SOL, token balances, allowances already confirmed, and for Solana the rent for any new ATAs. EVM fee spikes beyond the approved limits make execution fail rather than bump fees.

The transaction window shows raw data only (network, sender, destination, wei value, calldata). Users can't verify token effects there, so describe the action clearly in tool text without claiming PayBox verified it.

x402 via plugins: USDC only on Base or Solana mainnet, exact asset, GET or POST JSON of 64 KiB or less, no headers. The payer must be a plain EOA; a gasless swap that delegates the wallet via 7702 can break later x402 payments. The paid response returns through the PayBox request, and processing it needs another explicit plugin call.
Wallet selection: when the user has several compatible wallets, use_plugin needs wallet_id. The SDK and CLI cannot pass it, so CLI demos should grant only one compatible wallet per chain family.

Process: end-to-end agent testing only becomes possible after Submit Project, so submit an early version. Code is frozen after 8pm EDT Oct 17, but hosts, variables and secrets stay editable. Keep volatile logic in the backend while tool schemas stay stable.
Eligibility: submission may require MoonPay KYC with the same email as the PayBox account, and winners must pass KYC/AML. One project per individual.

Compliance and review: designs that move value through off-chain signatures (typed data relayed by the plugin) may look like they bypass the rule that plugin money tools always need approval. Prediction-market designs must respect geofencing; PayBox geofences its own World tools.
Mainnet costs: the demo needs real USDC on Base or Solana plus ETH or SOL for gas. Facilitator free tiers are limited (PayAI: 1,000 credits per receiving wallet); CDP needs API keys.
open_questions: Which exact eip155 chain IDs does the hosted proposal validator accept? Portal 'Validate transaction' is the only authoritative test. Are Robinhood 4663, Arc 5042, HyperEVM 999, Monad 143 and Celo 42220 accepted, and is Tempo (no native gas token) supported at all?

Do plugin x402 proposals support x402 v2 (PAYMENT-REQUIRED header) challenges, or only v1 JSON bodies? Which Solana x402 facilitators and fee-payer setups does PayBox accept, and is the 'upto' scheme rejected?
What timeout and maximum response size apply to PayBox's paid re-fetch for plugin x402 requests, and is a binary or non-JSON body passed to the agent intact?
Can a tool return extra structuredContent fields next to io.paybox/transactionProposal (for example quote metadata), or must the proposal be the only key, as in the strict starter schemas?
Does PayBox forward any per-user or per-installation identifier, or a stable egress IP and region, to plugin network hosts? This matters for rate limiting, geoblocked APIs and backend auth.
Is get_plugin a real core tool, distinct from get_contract, for unofficial or Open Plugins? What exactly are 'remote plugins' with a 'connected origin', and could a remote MCP server be submitted?
Will judges install and run the unofficial plugin themselves, or judge mainly from the X demo video? This changes how much effort should go into robustness versus the demo.
Does PayBox policy restrict or warn on agent-requested EIP-712 typed data (Permit, Permit2, EIP-3009) under autonomous grants? Would reviewers accept sign-then-relay plugin designs?
Do enabled unofficial plugin tools also appear directly in the host's tools/list (as official ones do), and how are they named in Claude.ai or ChatGPT?

Does ChatGPT web have connector quirks (developer-mode requirement, extra write-action confirmations, MCP Apps signing-window rendering) that would affect a live demo? This could not be verified because the web-search budget was exhausted mid-research.
